clue.text: Going asleep

parts.note: read 'going' as passing water and 'asleep' as while sleeping: a night-time accident

explanation.surface: Someone drifting off to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going' looks like 'becoming', as in going to sleep; here it is the euphemism for urinating, and 'asleep' says when it happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Wetting the bed is literally relieving oneself while sleeping, the euphemistic 'going' done in one's sleep.

clue.text: "Killing cat", a disastrous sort of ode

indicators.note: killing something gets rid of it, so these words are removed from the next word's synonym

parts.note: something disastrous is catastrophic
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim poem about a murdered cat, presented as a kind of ode.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killing' takes CAT and A off the front of CATASTROPHIC (disastrous), leaving the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A strophic poem is built of repeated stanzas, or strophes, the classic structure of a Greek choral ode.

clue.text: Drone, as it were, released inside stage of rocket

indicators.note: inside places the shuffled letters within the rocket stage

parts.note: a booster is the first stage of a rocket

indicators.note: released letters are set free to fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drone with something let loose within a section of a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drone' suggests a bee or an unmanned aircraft, but P. G. Wodehouse's hero is a member of the Drones Club, a London club for idle young men. 'released' shuffles the fodder; 'inside' sets it in the rocket stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's idle hero belongs to the Drones Club, and a drone is an idler living off others.

clue.text: See 8
Fairy liquid: pure, clean, capital for hands

indicators.note: a liquid flows and changes shape, so the letters before it are reshaped
the capital letter of a word is its initial

explanation.surface: Reads like an advert for Fairy Liquid, the washing-up brand, as pure and clean and great for your hands.
explanation.walkthrough: Fairy Liquid is a British washing-up liquid, so 'Fairy' seems a brand name. 'liquid' shuffles PURE, CLEAN and H, the capital of 'hands'.
explanation.definitionFit: A leprechaun is a mischievous little sprite of Irish folklore, a kind of fairy.

clue.text: Typical statesman, one making advances to Cameron

parts.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker, who advances money on pledged goods
Samantha Cameron, wife of the former Prime Minister David Cameron, is known as Sam

explanation.surface: A model politician who makes overtures to David Cameron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is a pawnbroker, one lending money against goods; Sam Cameron was the wife of the UK Prime Minister David Cameron.
explanation.definitionFit: This personification of the United States government stands for a stereotypical American, the States' typical man.

clue.text: Sort of saga which almost was related to 3 11

parts.note: an Aga saga is a genre of English middle-class family novel, named after the Aga cooker

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: which can be replaced by that

explanation.surface: A type of family saga that nearly connects to a famous fictional character.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a large range cooker found in English country kitchens, giving the 'Aga saga' novel. 'almost' trims THAT to THA.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunt Agatha is Bertie's formidable aunt in Wodehouse's stories, so she was a relation of his.

clue.text: Crosspiece put over hole in floor

indicators.note: put over means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a rood is a cross, and a piece is a part

explanation.surface: A crossbar laid across a gap in the floorboards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crosspiece' looks like one word for a beam; split it as cross, ROOD, plus piece, PART, then 'put over' turns ROODPART round.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapdoor is a hinged panel covering an opening in a floor or ceiling.

clue.text: Back in school cafe finally, really fancied horse meat

indicators.note: back means the whole assembled string is read in reverse
in places the horse within the school

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school
a cert is a horse thought sure to win

indicators.note: finally picks the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A school canteen serving up horse meat, presented as a delicacy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the horse inside the school and 'Back' reverses the whole string. A cert is British racing slang for a near-certain winner; Eton is England's best-known public school.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrecôte is a cut of beef steak taken from between the ribs.

clue.text: One African country or another loses excellent backing

indicators.note: loses says letters are dropped from the country

parts.note: Nigeria is another African country

indicators.note: backing means the word for excellent is read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written AI

explanation.surface: One African state, or a neighbour, losing first-class support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns AI (A1, excellent) into IA, and 'loses' strips IA from the end of NIGERIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Niger is a landlocked West African republic, neighbouring Nigeria to the north.

clue.text: See 3
Slattern moves head along desk

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word is shifted along to the end

parts.note: a slattern and a trollop are both old words for a slovenly woman

explanation.surface: A slovenly woman shuffles her head across a desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moves head along' sends the first letter, T, of TROLLOP to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll-top is a writing desk with a flexible slatted cover that slides up and down.

clue.text: Chuckle from man in shirt

indicators.note: in places the man within the shirt

parts.note: a tee is a T-shirt
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: A giggle coming from a fellow wearing a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A tee-hee is a titter or snigger, the sound of a suppressed laugh.

clue.text: Yob, for one, supports Fritz

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
Fritz Lang was the German film director of Metropolis

explanation.surface: A thug backs a German, Fritz being slang for a German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yob' is a British word for a lout, itself 'boy' spelt backwards, which is why it exemplifies this slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Back slang forms words by reversing them; yob is the best-known example, from boy.

clue.text: One in a billion, vegetable that produces blood cells

parts.note: b is an abbreviation for billion
taken as written
a marrow is a large green vegetable

explanation.surface: A rare vegetable that somehow makes blood cells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in a billion' sounds like rarity; read it as ONE following B (a billion). A marrow is a large courgette-like squash grown in British gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone marrow is the soft tissue inside bones where red and white blood cells are made.

clue.text: Order soldier to move unbriefed?

parts.note: go! is an order given to send someone off
a commando is a soldier trained for raids

explanation.surface: A command to a soldier to get moving, then a hint he lacks his briefing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unbriefed' looks like 'not given instructions'; it means without briefs, underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means wearing no underwear, so going about with no briefs on.

clue.text: Bars not essential in the theatre?

definitions.text: Bars not essential in the theatre?

parts.words: Bars not essential in the theatre
parts.note: bars are measures of music, and not essential means ... accompanying a play

explanation.surface: Theatre bars that you could do without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' in a theatre suggests the interval drinks counters; here they are bars of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Music written to accompany a stage play, secondary to the drama, is a background score.

clue.text: Painstaking cover-up — it protects dope

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: a lid is a cover

indicators.note: protects means the first word wraps around the second

parts.note: dope and gen both mean information

explanation.surface: A careful cover-up in which something shields drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover-up' looks like a scandal; in a down clue 'up' reverses the cover. 'protects' wraps 'it' round the dope, which is slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: A diligent worker is careful and thorough, taking pains over the job.

clue.text: Oral exam headed by teacher one gets through

indicators.note: oral means spoken, so the words are said out loud

parts.note: sir is how a teacher is addressed, put before viva, an oral exam

explanation.surface: A spoken exam opened by the teacher, with one candidate passing.
explanation.walkthrough: A viva is a spoken university exam. SIR VIVA, said in a non-rhotic British accent, matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A survivor is someone who comes through an ordeal alive, getting through it.

clue.text: Originally meant to hang, free old highwayman

indicators.note: originally means arranged in an original, novel way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A highwayman first sentenced to hang, then freed long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' looks like the anagram signal but its letters are needed; 'Originally' reorders MEANT TO HANG FREE OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a polite euphemism for a mounted robber who held up travellers on the highway.

clue.text: One old tatty ribbon

indicators.note: tatty means scruffy and disordered, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A single worn, shabby ribbon.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is a long flat strip of pasta, a ribbon of dough.

clue.text: Endless delight, alcohol in a big bowl

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: joy is delight
rum is an alcoholic spirit

explanation.surface: Unending pleasure from drink in a large bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims JOY to JO.
explanation.definitionFit: A jorum is an old word for a large drinking bowl or its contents, often of punch.

parts.note: the clue reads as Bertie Wooster's gentleman's gentleman, the term for a valet

explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the cross-references: 3 11 is Bertie Wooster and 19 is gentleman, giving a gentleman's gentleman, a valet.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's unflappable valet serves Bertie in the stories, a manservant being called a gentleman's gentleman.

clue.text: Fine given by Recorder, who would prefer harsher punishment?

parts.note: f stands for fine, as on pencil leads
a logger records data

explanation.surface: A magistrate's fine, imposed by a judge who would rather have been tougher.
explanation.walkthrough: A Recorder is a part-time judge in England, which steers the reading toward courts.
explanation.definitionFit: A flogger is one who favours corporal punishment, wanting whipping rather than fines.

clue.text: In Jane's good books, offering sweets

indicators.note: in at the start says the following books go inside the actress's name

parts.note: Jane Fonda is the American actress; with the 's it gives a possessive
NT is the New Testament, books of the Good Book

explanation.surface: Someone in Jane's good graces, handing out sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Jane's good books' looks like the idiom for being in favour. Instead Jane is the actress Jane Fonda, keeping her 'S, and 'In' puts the New Testament inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondants are soft creamy confections made from sugar paste, a kind of sweet.

clue.text: From a kingdom of Anglo-Saxons, I moved to 6's land

indicators.note: moved means a letter is shifted to another position

parts.note: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the English Midlands
taken as written

explanation.surface: An emigrant from old Mercia, travelling to the New World.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I moved' shifts the I in A MERCIA one place along. 6 is Uncle Sam, the personified USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam personifies the United States, so his land is that country.

clue.text: See 22
Fibre is new, only just spun

indicators.note: spun means twisted around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fibre that has been freshly spun.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic polymer made into threads for textiles.

clue.text: See 19
